recall_prompt: Say how you would resolve (x + 4)/((x² − 4)(x + 1)) into partial fractions — name each move in order.
insider_note: x² − 4 is not irreducible — it splits as (x + 2)(x − 2), so the denominator is three different linear factors with three constants, and each root gives one of them directly.

steps.label: Set up the form
steps.margin_note: First mark. x² − 4 is a difference of squares, so the denominator has THREE different linear factors: (x + 2), (x − 2), (x + 1). Three factors, three constants.
steps.memory_tip: x² − 4 is a difference of squares, so it SPLITS: three different linear factors, three constants.

recall.must_convey: That x² − 4 is factorised as (x + 2)(x − 2) and the fraction is written as A/(x + 2) + B/(x − 2) + C/(x + 1).
accept: factorise x squared minus four as x plus two into x minus two and write A over x plus two plus B over x minus two plus C over x plus one
three linear factors so three constants A B and C one over each factor
split it into A by x plus 2 plus B by x minus 2 plus C by x plus 1
x square minus four ni x plus two, x minus two ga factorise chesi A B C ni one over each factor ga rasali
write one constant over each of the three factors x plus two x minus two and x plus one

steps.why: x² − 4 looks like a quadratic factor but it is not irreducible: it splits into (x + 2)(x − 2). Missing that gives a (Bx + C)/(x² − 4) form that is not wrong but is harder and is not what the examiner expects.
common_mistakes: Treating x² − 4 as an irreducible quadratic and writing (Bx + C)/(x² − 4).
Writing only two constants for three factors.

steps.label: Clear the denominators
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Multiply by all three factors. Each constant keeps the two factors that are NOT its own. The C term keeps (x + 2)(x − 2), which is x² − 4 again.
steps.memory_tip: Each constant keeps the two factors that are not its own. The C term keeps (x + 2)(x − 2).

recall.must_convey: That multiplying through gives x + 4 = A(x − 2)(x + 1) + B(x + 2)(x + 1) + C(x + 2)(x − 2).
accept: multiply both sides by all three factors so x plus four equals A into x minus two into x plus one plus B into x plus two into x plus one plus C into x plus two into x minus two
clear the denominators and each constant keeps the two factors that are not its own
multiply through by the whole denominator to get an identity in x
moodu factors tho multiply cheste x plus four equals A into the other two factors plus B into the other two plus C into the other two
remove all the fractions by multiplying with x plus two x minus two x plus one

steps.why: With three fractions the identity has three products, and each product is the denominator with one factor removed. Writing it once, correctly, is what makes the three substitutions in the next step work.
common_mistakes: Giving A the factor (x + 2) that it sits over; A keeps (x − 2)(x + 1).
Losing the left side x + 4 and writing only the right side.

steps.label: Find the constants
steps.margin_note: Third mark. Three roots, three substitutions: x = −2 for A, x = 2 for B, x = −1 for C. Each one makes the other two terms zero. Watch the signs in the brackets.
steps.memory_tip: Three roots, three substitutions: −2, 2, −1. Watch the signs — (−2 − 2)(−2 + 1) = (−4)(−1) = +4.

recall.must_convey: That x = −2 gives A = 1/2, x = 2 gives B = 1/2 and x = −1 gives C = −1.
accept: put x equals minus two to get A equals half, x equals two to get B equals half and x equals minus one to get C equals minus one
substitute the three roots minus two two and minus one to get A half B half and C minus one
A is half B is half and C is minus one from the three substitutions
x equals minus two pedithe A half, x equals two pedithe B half, x equals minus one pedithe C minus one
each root makes two terms zero so A and B are half and C is minus one

steps.why: Each substitution is chosen to be the root of one factor, so two of the three products vanish and one constant is left multiplied by a known number. Three roots give three constants with no simultaneous equations.
common_mistakes: Writing (−2 − 2)(−2 + 1) as (−4)(1) instead of (−4)(−1), which flips the sign of A.
Getting 12B = 6 and writing B = 2 instead of 1/2.
Forgetting the third substitution and leaving C unfound.

steps.label: Write the result
steps.margin_note: Last mark. A = 1/2 over (x + 2) is written as 1/(2(x + 2)); the 2 goes into the denominator. The minus on C becomes a minus between the fractions.
steps.memory_tip: A = 1/2 over (x + 2) is written 1/(2(x + 2)), with the 2 inside the denominator. Check x = 0: 4 = −1 + 1 + 4.

steps.why: The examiner marks the resolved form. Writing 1/2 over a bracket as 1/(2(x + 2)) is the standard way to present a fractional constant and keeps the answer on one line.
common_mistakes: Writing C = −1 as +1/(x + 1) in the final line.
Writing (1/2)/(x + 2) with a stacked half; put the 2 in the denominator instead.
Not checking: put x = 0 in the identity, 4 = −1 + 1 + 4. If the two sides differ, a constant is wrong.
